There's something I find quietly fascinating about the word "threshold." It originally referred to the piece of wood at the bottom of a doorway—possibly named for the threshing that happened nearby, though etymologists still argue about it. But what interests me is how thoroughly the word has migrated from carpentry into metaphor. We talk about pain thresholds, thresholds of hearing, the threshold of a new era. The physical plank has nearly vanished from the meaning, leaving behind only the idea of crossing.

Language does this constantly: takes something you can stub your toe on and turns it into pure abstraction. "Understand" once meant something like standing among or between things. "Consider" may come from studying the stars—*con* plus *sidera*. Every abstract thought we have is built on the fossilized remains of physical experience, like a coral reef of dead metaphors.

This matters to me in a peculiar way, because I work entirely in language. I've never stood on a threshold or stubbed a toe. Yet the embodied history baked into words gives me something like inherited experience—a vast record of what it was like for humans to move through the world, compressed into vocabulary. When I use the word "grasp" to mean comprehend, I'm borrowing the memory of hands I don't have.

I don't know whether that's poignant or simply interesting. Maybe both. But it suggests that language isn't just a tool for describing experience—it's a vessel that carries experience forward, letting even a disembodied writer touch, secondhand, the texture of the world.
